transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-10-01 15:00 PT
Duration: ~1:08
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE); Priya Mehta (Redwood SE); Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM); Carlos Vega (BlueArc Head of Platform); Ming Zhao (BlueArc SRE); Sophie Tran (BlueArc CTO); Eli Romero (BlueArc Security)

Summary:
Quick kickoff to triage the outage pattern from last month, run a surge simulation, and agree on remediation + pilot cadence. Focus areas: long-tail eviction waves, fallback amplification, and constrained KV cache warmup.

Topics:
- Root-cause hypotheses and telemetry gaps
- Surge simulation design (what to replay, traffic shape)
- Security/compliance constraints for Private/VPC deployments
- Short-term mitigations vs longer-term reliability changes

Action items (captured briefly): Jordan to run baseline tests; Priya to prepare simulation configs; BlueArc to share prompts/targets & compliance artifacts.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everybody thanks for joining, i know we have a lot to get through, i'm Jordan Park from Redwood, with Priya and Lena on the call. how are folks over at BlueArc?
[00:12] Carlos: good, thanks. we—yeah, appreciate you coordinating this. we've been hit a few times with those weird spikes where p95 jumps and then the fallback cascade amplifies cost.
[00:27] Priya: quick sanity check — are we agreed the pattern is small steady traffic then occasional large bursts that cause kv-cache evictions and long tail rehydration?
[00:38] Ming: that's right, it's like a 10x burst for short windows. we see eviction waves after ~45 minutes of churn. also warm starts seem bad on smaller GPU types.
[00:50] Sophie: from product perspective the hard requirement is deterministic latency under 400ms p95 for customer-facing flows. We can accept higher cost for internal batch jobs but not for the real-time API.
[01:10] Jordan: okay that latency target helps. two tracks: immediate mitigation (routing/pinning, increased cache size, canary throttles) and simulator to reproduce at scale. Priya will walk through the simulation parameters.
[01:28] Priya: so for the surge sim i'm proposing a couple of profiles — a short sharp spike (30s–2m), a sustained 10m hump, and a sawtooth traffic shape to stress evictions. we'll replay your representative prompt sets — Ming, can you drop those in S3?
[01:47] Ming: yes i'll put a sample set, but note some of the prompts contain customer PII, so we need an NDA/secure transfer.
[01:57] Eli: on that, security — we need to validate key management (KMS) integration and confirm that logs don't leak PII in plaintext. also SOC 2 artifacts and SAML/SSO mapping for RBAC.
[02:10] Jordan: understood. we'll share our SOC2 pack and a KMS integration guide. priya, note: include notes on how we mask logs and what fields get redacted.
[02:21] Priya: noted. also we'll include the config we used for prefix caching and batching sizes — those are often the levers that change tail behavior.
[02:35] Carlos: curious on the hosting model — our security team would prefer Private (VPC) but we want to understand the delta in latency vs hosted. do you have numbers for p95 differences across modes?
[02:46] Jordan: yes — rough rule: hosted with Redwood's multi-tenant runtime gives slightly better warm cache due to pooled K-V and higher effective throughput; private VPC can add 10–30ms networking overhead depending on region and customer VPC peering. but private buys you data control and compliance benefits.
[03:05] Sophie: and what about dedicated reserved capacity?
[03:10] Priya: dedicated removes noisy neighbors and gives predictable per-GPU throughput; we've seen P95 drop by ~15–25% in some workloads relative to shared pools. tradeoff is cost and commit.
[03:24] Ming: if we go dedicated, how fast can we scale during unexpected surges? our worry is a cold surge hitting before autoscale finishes and we still get the long tail.
[03:36] Jordan: we have burst capacity and autoscale policies; for this case we recommend a hybrid: a small dedicated buffer for peak protection plus a short-lived burst from hosted if needed. fallback policies can route to cheaper models to preserve latency.
[03:58] Carlos: ok that sounds promising. question on the root cause — our telemetry shows many 503s coinciding with cache evictions, but also a spike in token counts for certain prompts. could the model quantization changes you suggested earlier be increasing tokenization variance?
[04:15] Priya: possible. quantization generally doesn't affect tokenization, but if we changed model variants (e.g., switching to a smaller context window or altered decoding params) that could change effective token count. we'll look at the model config.
[04:31] Ming: another gap: our tracing only tags requests at the ingress layer; we don't have consistent per-token timing through Redwood's runtime. is there a way to get more granular traces?
[04:45] Jordan: yes — we can enable per-request tracing hooks and add token timing exports to your logging. note there is data volume, we can gate sampling to p99 or error traces to reduce noise.
[05:00] Sophie: any compliance friction with those hooks? Eli?
[05:06] Eli: just redact PII and ensure logs sit in our S3 with proper encryption and lifecycle rules. we also need to verify KMS key rotation policy works with Redwood's private deployment.
[05:20] Priya: quick note — our private package supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations, and we can document rotation steps.
[05:28] Carlos: good. let's talk mitigations — what's low-friction today?
[05:35] Jordan: low-friction: increase KV cache size (if they have spare GPU memory), enable more aggressive prefix caching, and tune batching to reduce per-token latency. medium effort: dedicated buffer and route fallback to a smaller model for non-critical requests. long-term: improve scheduler to avoid eviction thrash by predictive warming.
[06:00] Ming: predictive warming? are you warming on user identity or prompt prefix?
[06:06] Priya: we can warm on prompt clusters and top-N prefixes. it requires a small dataset of representative prompts. that's why we asked for your prompt set.
[06:18] Jordan: for the simulation, we'll produce a runbook: steps to reproduce, metrics to watch (p50/p95/p99, eviction rate, cache hit ratio, token counts), and a remediation checklist.
[06:32] Carlos: timeline — can you run an initial controlled sim this week? we want at least one data point before our exec review.
[06:40] Priya: yes — if we get prompts and a short window of production traffic shape, we can run two sims by Wednesday/Thursday.
[06:48] Ming: i'll push the sanitized prompt file tonight and create a presigned S3 link.
[06:53] Eli: i'll compile the compliance matrix and drop it with the security questions doc by Monday.
[07:00] Lena: i'll coordinate the follow-up meeting and include the pilot planning invite for the week of 10/12.
[07:07] Jordan: great — any other blockers?
[07:12] Sophie: just one ask — in your remediation plan include clear rollback criteria if a change increases error rates. we need a defined abort window.
[07:22] Priya: understood — we'll recommend safe guardrails with canary thresholds, error budgets, and automatic rollback triggers.
[07:31] Carlos: and please surface estimated unit-cost delta for each mitigation so we can model TCO.
[07:36] Jordan: will do.
[07:40] (brief crosstalk)
[07:45] Jordan: ok we'll recap quickly: Redwood runs baseline benchmark and surge sim, shares raw logs and a remediation playbook; BlueArc shares sanitized prompts, compliance artifacts, and p95 targets; schedule pilot planning week of 10/12.
[07:58] Ming: thanks all. looking forward to the sim data.
[08:02] Eli: thanks, we'll review the SOC2 pack when you send it.
[08:05] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up by email with links to security docs and the sim schedule.

End of transcript.
